title: County of Touraine
capsule: The County of Touraine was a medieval French territorial lordship centered on Tours in the Loire valley, historically dominated by the Counts of Blois and then the Angevin dynasty from 1044. When the Angevins became kings of England in 1154, Touraine formed a central component of the Plantagenet continental domain, with the castle at Chinon serving as a principal stronghold. Philip II Augustus of France recaptured the county in 1205 following the collapse of Angevin power north of the Loire, after which it was administered as a royal appanage and elevated to a duchy. Its existence as a distinct administrative entity ended during the French Revolution when the 1790 reorganization dissolved historic provinces into departments, Touraine becoming primarily Indre-et-Loire.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. The county's territorial core is well-established; medieval boundaries with neighboring counties (Anjou, Blois, Berry) are approximately known from feudal documents but not precisely mapped.
